sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in
sources.note: KAMASAU (kama1367), NOT Elepi. Sect. 4 word, pp. 114-115: 'Stress tends to occur in one of the two first syllables of a word. Stress is not contrastive between words.. Stress in disyllabic words tends to occur on the initial syllable. However, stress may occur on the final syllable under the following conditions: (1) an open final syllable with a complex nucleus containing a back vowel.. (2) a word-final closed syllable whose final consonant is bilabial, velar or glottal'; 3-4 syllable words 'have not fallen into a distinct pattern', tentatively initial unless the second syllable has a back v…

A secondhand coverage bibliography: for Elepi it lists only Laycock 1973 and Sanders & Sanders 1980a (both already read and silent), i.e. no phonology, sketch, grammar or dictionary existed for Elepi as of 2012; useful only as an independent confirmation that the Glottolog list is complete and that Gehberger 1950 belongs to Austronesian Terebu/Kaiep, not Elepi.

sources.citation: Sanders, Arden G. & Joy Sanders. 1980. Defining the centres of the Marienberg language family. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 20, Pacific Linguistics A-56: 171-196. DOI 10.15144/PL-A56.171
sources.note: Nothing. Lexicostatistic/sociolinguistic survey of the six Marienberg languages; Elepi = one village (Samap), 179 speakers; pronoun/verb-prefix comparison table p. 195. No phonology, no stress.
sources.venue: Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 20, Pacific Linguistics A-56: 171-196

sources.citation: Sanders, Joy & Arden G. Sanders. 1980. Dialect survey of the Kamasau language. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 20, Pacific Linguistics A-56: 137-170. DOI 10.15144/PL-A56.137
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Includes Samap (= Elepi, note 1 p. 168) in the Kamasau survey; pp. 146-147 give only segmental correspondences for Samap vs Tring/Yibab-Wandomi (stop voicing, Tring s ~ Samap t, glottals retained, e > a, o > a). The only first-hand phonological notes on Elepi found anywhere; silent on stress. Extracted from the ANU volume PDF because the ANU item-level bitstream for this paper is mislinked.
sources.venue: Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 20, Pacific Linguistics A-56: 137-170

sources.citation: Laycock, Donald C. 1973. Sepik languages: checklist and preliminary classification. Pacific Linguistics B-25. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Nothing. Entry 53 ELEPI (Samap, Sumup), pp. 16-17, gives only village, test list DCL71, the naming rationale (elepi = 'there are none') and the remark that Elepi 'is very closely related to Kamasau, but seems more than just a dialect'. No phonological data.
